Ecology
Ecology is the study of the relationship between organisms and their environments.
In this unit, we will study ecology by focusing on how matter and energy are transferred through the organisms and their environment
Earth as a Closed System
There are three types of systems:
Open System: An open system exchanges both matter and energy with its surroundings.
Closed System: A closed system exchanges energy but not matter with its surroundings.
Isolated System: An isolated system neither exchanges matter nor energy with its surroundings.

Earth is considered a closed system because it exchanges energy (e.g., sunlight enters, and heat radiates out into space) but not significant amounts of matter. While some small particles, like meteoroids, enter, and gases occasionally escape into space, these exchanges are negligible compared to the overall system.
Earth’s Sphere
The biosphere is the part of the Earth and its atmosphere in which living organisms exist or that is capable of supporting life.
The atmosphere is the layer of gases that surrounds and protects the Earth, providing air and regulating temperature.
The lithosphere (or geosphere) is the solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth, including the crust and upper mantle.
The hydrosphere encompasses all water on Earth, whether in liquid, solid, or vapor form, including oceans, rivers, glaciers, and clouds.
All organisms need energy to live...
According to the first law of thermodynamics, energy cannot be created or destroyed.
So where does this energy come from? And where does it go? This is what we are going to explore next.
Energy Flow
Nearly 100% of the Earth’s energy comes from the sun
Not all of the sun’s energy, however, reaches the Earth’s surface.
Much of the incoming solar radiation (~30%) is reflected from clouds, dust particles, as well as water and land surfaces.
Some (~19%) is absorbed by atmosphere and clouds.
About 50% does reach the surface where it gets absorbed, only about 1-2% of the total incoming energy is used by photosynthetic producers (e.g. plants)
Albedo
Albedo refers to the amount of energy reflected by clouds, water, and land.
High albedo, means more energy is reflected. White and light surfaces reflect more light, therefore they have a high albedo. (e.g. snow)
Low albedo means less energy is reflected. Black and dark surfaces absorb more energy, therefore reflect less, and have a low albedo. (e.g. soil)
Albedo and Climate Change
Melting Ice and Snow: Ice and snow reflect a lot of sunlight. As they melt due to warming, darker surfaces like oceans and land absorb more heat, making the planet warmer.
Thawing Permafrost: When frozen ground melts, darker soil is exposed, absorbing more sunlight.
Changing Vegetation: Warmer climates can turn snowy areas into forests or shrubs, which absorb more sunlight.
Climate change has reduced Earth's albedo, which is how much sunlight the planet reflects.
Albedo and Climate Change
Clouds and Pollution: Pollution can make clouds more reflective, but climate change also alters cloud patterns, which affects how much sunlight is reflected.
Ocean Absorption: Melting sea ice reveals dark ocean water, which absorbs more heat and speeds up warming.
All these changes mean Earth absorbs more sunlight, which makes global warming even worse, which lowers the albedo even further in a positive feedback loop.

We know that energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can, however, be converted into different forms. Radiant energy from the sun that does reach the earth is converted into various forms of usable energy by living things...

A portion of the sun’s energy that does reach the ground is used by producers for photosynthesis
Photosynthesis is the process by which producers (plants, algae, and some bacteria) convert radiant (light) energy from the sun into chemical potential energy (lot more on this in Unit C)
Chemical energy is stored in the bonds of carbohydrate molecules known as glucose, or sugar, which may then be used to fuel cellular activities
Because producers use the sun’s energy to create their own glucose (food) they are also referred to as “autotrophs”

Photosynthesis:
Radiant energy converted to chemical energy (stored in the chemical bonds of glucose)
A different kind of producer
In the absence of light, microorganisms who dwell near deep-sea vents use hydrogen sulfide (H2S) molecules to produce their own carbohydrate-based energy...
This process is known as chemosynthesis, and results in the production of sulfuric acid instead of oxygen.

What about organisms who cannot produce their own food???
Consumers must obtain their food (glucose) by eating producers (or other consumers)
Because consumers obtain their energy from other organisms, they are also referred to as “heterotrophs”.

Characterization of Consumers
Primary Consumers
Organisms that eat plants (herbivores)
e.g. some insects, zooplankton, grazing mammals, mammals that eat fruit & seeds, some species of birds and fish
Secondary Consumers
Organisms that mainly eat herbivores (can be omnivores or carnivores)
e.g. spiders, frogs, insect-eating birds
Tertiary Consumers
Organisms that mainly eat other carnivores (true carnivores)
e.g. lions, wolves, polar bears, eagles
Decomposers
Decomposers can’t make their own food, but also do not exactly consume/eat other organisms the same way as typical consumers do
Decomposers instead break down wastes and decaying materials and absorb nutrients from that
e.g. fungi, bacteria, worms, some insects
E.g. mushrooms secrete special digestive juices into their surroundings, that break down complex organic molecules into smaller soluble molecules that the fungi then absorb
Decomposers thus serve a critical role in ecosystems, by returning nutrients into the soil so producers can use them again
Decomposers
Decomposers are essential because they recycle nutrients back into ecosystems, maintaining the balance of life.
Since Earth is a closed system, we have a finite amount of matter and nutrients available, which need to be recycled.

By breaking down dead plants, animals, and organic waste, they release nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, and carbon into the soil and atmosphere, making them available for plants and other organisms to use.
Without decomposers, ecosystems would accumulate dead material, and nutrient cycles would break down, disrupting the growth and survival of living organisms.

Now that we observed where each organisms gets its food (glucose) from, what’s next? Glucose is just a storage molecule for energy, organisms can not actually use glucose directly to fuel bodily processes.

Through a process known as cellular respiration, both producers and consumers (and most decomposers) convert the chemical energy stored in the bonds of glucose into ATP molecules which serve as our body’s main fuel source. (more on this in Unit C)
Cellular Respiration
Chemical energy converted into kinetic & heat energy
Interdependence
Producers & consumers are intrinsically linked through the processes of photosynthesis and cell respiration…
Tracking the transfer of food and energy
A food chain shows the linear pathway through which food is transferred from producers to primary consumers and to progressively higher feeding levels.
Food webs are are interlocking food chains that illustrate more complex feeding relationships between organisms.
Note: the arrow points to the eater and shows the transfer of energy.
Trophic levels simply refer to the feeding levels in an ecosystem through which energy and matter are transferred...
The first trophic level provides all the chemical energy required to fuel the other trophic levels (producers)
All remaining trophic levels consist of consumers
Decomposers may feed at any of the trophic levels
Efficiency in Ecosystems
Food webs show the flow of energy and nutrients in an ecosystem. Matter cannot be lost but energy is “lost” in the transformation process.
This loss of energy limits the number of trophic levels that a food web can contain to no more than six.
In all food chains/food webs, the amount of available energy decreases as you move up the chain.
So why is energy transfer so inefficient?
Where does the Energy Go?
Most of the energy produced by autotrophs is used to promote the survival and growth of the organism.
Consumers don’t process all of the food they eat.  Some is eliminated through waste. (i.e. pooped out)
Some of the energy taken in by a consumer is required to acquire, digest and metabolize the food eaten.
Much of the energy metabolized is also lost as heat. (Second Law of Thermodynamics)
Exactly how much energy is transferred from one trophic level to another?
The efficiency with which energy is transferred through trophic levels varies among different kinds of organisms…
Generally, ecologists assume that 10 percent of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next trophic level.
Thus, approximately 90% of energy is lost with each step. This is referred to as the “Rule of 10”.
To calculate the energy available at each level, we can calculate 10% of the previous energy, or just simply divide by 10.
Rule of 10
Taking into consideration the Rule of 10, does it make more sense to maintain a mostly vegetarian diet, or one that consists mostly of meat?
“Planetary Health Diet”
Energy is lost from a food chain at each step. Therefore, it is always more efficient to feed at lower trophic levels, as more energy transferred from the Sun.

Pyramids of Numbers
Because more energy is available to lower trophic levels, the number of producers often greatly outnumbers the number of consumers in an ecosystem
This pattern results in a pyramid of numbers, with each bar of the pyramid representing the number of organisms in each trophic level

2) Pyramids of Biomass
Biomass represent the dry mass of living organisms per unit area (imagine if you evaporated all the water from an organism, dry mass is what would remain)
A better demonstration of how energy is transferred from one trophic level to another, as it takes into account the actual size of organisms in an ecosystem rather than just the number.

Biogeochemical Cycles

A biogeochemical cycle is the natural process that moves elements and compounds through living organisms (bio), the Earth's surface (geo), and the atmosphere (chemical). These cycles ensure that essential nutrients are continuously recycled and available for life.
In biogeochemical cycles, nutrients (water, carbon, phosphorus, etc.) move through various storage locations called reservoirs.
E.g. ocean for water, atmosphere for nitrogen, living things for carbon, etc.
We will look at the following 5 biogeochemical cycles
Water cycle (hydrologic cycle)
Carbon (and oxygen) cycle
Nitrogen cycle
Sulphur cycle
Phosphorus Cycle
The Hydrologic Cycle
The hydrologic cycle involves all phases of water. It is the cycling of water that connects ecosystems across the globe.
Liquid water in lakes/ponds/oceans is turned into a gas through evaporation (or transpiration if the water is from the leaves of plants).
Water vapour in the atmosphere condenses in clouds.
Liquid water returns to the ground through precipitation (e.g. snow/rain)
Water re-enters lakes/ponds/oceans through run-off. .
Some of the water infiltrates into the soil and makes its way to ground storage and eventually to lakes and oceans.
Water for Life
Water is a polar molecule, meaning it has an uneven distribution of charge. The oxygen atom has a slight negative charge, while the hydrogen atoms have a slight positive charge.
This polarity allows water molecules to form hydrogen bonds with each other.
These weak yet significant bonds contribute to water’s high boiling point, high surface tension, and ability to dissolve many substances. Without these properties, life as we know it wouldn’t exist.
Water is known as the "universal solvent" because it dissolves more substances than any other liquid. This is due to its polarity, which allows it to surround and separate charged or polar molecules.
This makes it essential for biological processes, such as transporting nutrients in blood, dissolving waste, and enabling chemical reactions in cells.
It also plays a role in weathering rocks, releasing minerals that sustain ecosystems.
Observe how water molecules pull away other polar or charged particles due to the attraction of positive and negative sides
Water is the Universal Solvent
Water has a High Specific Heat Capacity
Water has a high specific heat capacity, meaning it takes a lot of energy to change its temperature. This happens because hydrogen bonds absorb heat without breaking easily.
This stabilizes temperatures in oceans and lakes, creating a more consistent environment for aquatic life.
It also helps regulate body temperature in organisms, preventing sudden overheating or cooling. For example, human bodies are about 60% water, which helps maintain a stable internal temperature.
Water’s Density Anomaly

Unlike most substances, water expands when it freezes, making ice less dense than liquid water. This is because hydrogen bonds lock water molecules into a crystalline structure with more space between them.
Since ice floats, it forms an insulating layer on lakes and oceans, preventing them from freezing solid in cold climates. This protects marine life and maintains aquatic ecosystems.
Without this property, bodies of water would freeze from the bottom up, making life in cold environments nearly impossible.
Nutrient Cycling in Lakes
Water is most dense at 4 degrees Celsius, and as lakes heat and cool throughout the seasons, water will cycle and thus redistribute nutrients:
Summer – Warm water stays on top, cold water at the bottom. No mixing, so nutrients sink.
Fall – Surface water cools to 4°C, sinks, and mixes the lake, bringing up nutrients and spreading oxygen.
Winter – Ice forms on top, but deeper water stays at 4°C. Little mixing happens.
Spring – Ice melts, surface water warms to 4°C, sinks, and mixes the lake again, refreshing nutrients and oxygen.
Cohesion refers to water molecules sticking to each other due to hydrogen bonding. This creates surface tension, which allows certain insects (like water striders) to walk on water.

Adhesion is water’s ability to stick to other substances. This is crucial for capillary action, which allows water to move up narrow tubes, like the xylem in plants. Without this, plants wouldn’t be able to transport water from their roots to their leaves, disrupting the entire food chain.
Cohesion and Adhesion
Some insects can walk on water
Beading of water
Cohesion and adhesion work together to transport water up the tissues of plants in a process called transpiration
Water is an essential part of life...
Obviously water plays an important role in distributing minerals and nutrients throughout our planet. However, water itself is also required to support the cellular activities of most living things.
Access to clean freshwater is thus essential for the success of many living things
The adult human body is composed of ~70% water;
many plants near 95% water
Metabolic activities require the constant balance of water consumption, retention, and loss
Other Roles of Water
Water & the Greenhouse Effect
When water is scarce due to drought or extreme heat, plants respond by closing their stomata, which reduces transpiration (this strategy is often utilized by desert plants, such as cacti)
Closed stomata mean that plants cannot take in carbon dioxide, slowing the rate of photosynthesis
What does this mean for atmospheric carbon dioxide levels during times of drought???
This would lead to a further increase in CO2 levels, making the problem of global warming even worse.
A Vicious Cycle...

The hydrologic cycle interacts with all other cycles of matter—such as the carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus cycles—by transporting nutrients, enabling chemical reactions, and sustaining ecosystems through the continuous movement of water across Earth's systems.
Thus, any change in the hydrologic cycle will affect other cycles of matter.
Other cycles of matter…
CARBON CYCLE
Carbon plays a key role in metabolic processes (cellular respiration & photosynthesis); is thus directly linked to the oxygen cycle
Moves from producer to consumer & decomposer, and back to the atmosphere through rapid cycling
CARBON CYCLE

Carbon also accumulates and is stored in various reservoirs for long periods of time, where it is unavailable to organisms until it is released. This cycling through carbon sinks is referred to as slow cycling.
Carbon sinks include trees, fossil fuel deposits, the ocean, and limestone rock.
Carbon is released from these reservoirs both quickly (e.g. forest fires) and slowly (e.g. weathering) through natural processes
CARBON CYCLE
How might human activity influence the cycling of carbon?
Deforestation reduces the number of trees that absorb CO₂ through photosynthesis, leading to higher atmospheric carbon levels and disrupting the carbon cycle.
Burning of fossil fuels releases large amounts of stored carbon from coal, oil, and natural gas into the atmosphere as CO₂, intensifying the greenhouse effect and climate change.
Industrial processes such as cement production and manufacturing emit CO₂ and other greenhouse gases, further altering the natural carbon balance and contributing to global warming.
NITROGEN CYCLE
Nitrogen makes up ~78% of earth’s atmosphere, and is an essential component of our genetic material (DNA); however, most organisms cannot actually use atmospheric nitrogen (N2)
Bacteria convert nitrogen gas into ammonia (NH3) through a process called nitrogen fixation.

Ammonia is still not readily usable by most plants,  and is converted by nitrifying bacteria into nitrites (NO2-) and finally nitrates (NO3-) during a process called nitrification. Nitrates can be easily taken up by plants from the soil.
Lightning can also fix nitrogen directly forming nitrates.
Animals can only obtain nitrogen by eating plants.
Excess nitrates in the soil are converted back into atmospheric nitrogen by a different set of bacteria. This process is known as denitrification.
Nitrogen fixation
NITROGEN CYCLE
How can we maintain nitrate levels in the soil??
Fertilizers may add nitrates to the soil, but they are a temporary (and costly) solution. The addition of nitrogen-fixing bacteria through crop cycling ensures a continuous supply of nitrates...
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria are often found in association with the roots of legume plants, such as clover and alfalfa. They live in the nodules found on their roots.
The bacteria convert nitrogen into ammonium for the plants, and the plants provide the bacteria with sugars produced through photosynthesis
SULFUR CYCLE
Sulfur-containing compounds are found primarily in the ground in the form of rocks, coal and oil…
Through volcanic activity, geologic uplift, or the mining & burning of fossil fuels, sulfur is then released into the air in the form of sulfur dioxide (SO2)
Sulfates do not stay in the air for very long; they are returned to the earth through acid precipitation (caused primarily by the burning of fossil fuels)
Bacteria in the soil then allow the sulfates to be used by plants. These sulfur compounds return to the soil once the plants die and decompose
Some of the sulfur returned to the ground is also re-deposited in rocks, and the cycle continues
SULFUR CYCLE
Acid deposition (or acid rain) occurs when slow-cycled sulfur deposited in rocks, oil, or coal is released into the atmosphere
Although acid deposition is a natural part of the sulfur cycle, large amounts can damage plants, acidify lakes, and leach nutrients from the soil

The amount of sulfur that is released due to human activities (such as the burning of fossil fuels) is far greater than the amount that is released through natural processes (such as weathering or volcanic activity)
SULFUR CYCLE
What’s that smell??
The distinctive “rotten egg” smell of sulfur is caused by decomposers who are hard at work producing hydrogen sulfide gas
H2S can be dangerous in high concentrations… thankfully, it’s easy to detect because of the smell
PHOSPHORUS CYCLE
Phosphorus is an essential nutrient (component of our bones and teeth), but it is found in limited quantities within the environment
Does not cycle through the atmosphere; instead, is found in soil and water. Often added to crops as fertilizer.
Weathering gradually releases phosphorus trapped in rocks
PHOSPHORUS CYCLE and EUTROPHICATION
While animals can obtain phosphorus by eating foods such as milk, grains, and meat, plants can only use phosphorus in the form of phosphates, which dissolve readily in water...
Although the scarcity of phosphorus keeps the growth of producers in check, it also limits the growth of crops
Large amounts of phosphates (and to a lesser extent nitrates), often from the overuse of fertilizers, can enter lakes and cause the water to be too rich in nutrients. This is called eutrophication.
Eutrophication can be harmful, leading to the overgrowth of algae, called an algal bloom
PHOSPHORUS CYCLE and EUTROPHICATION
As oxygen levels drop dramatically due to the above reasons, fish begin to die as well, further contributing to the growth of decomposers and the decrease of oxygen.
Eventually this vicious cycle can lead to the the entire lake dying off.
Algal blooms can block out sunlight from reaching plants underwater causing them to die, reducing dissolved oxygen levels.
Algae also do not photosynthesis at night, and instead of producing oxygen they use up a lot for cellular respiration.
When nutrients run out, the algae begin to die as well.
Decomposers will thrive breaking down plants and algae, but will consume further oxygen
The Biosphere in Balance
Did our atmosphere and oceans always have the same composition as today?
Deposits of ancient micro-organisms hold clues about the composition of the Earth’s atmosphere and oceans from 3.8 to 2.5 billion years ago
3.8 billion years ago the atmosphere lacked free oxygen.  Bacteria and bacteria-like organisms grew forming thick mounds in shallow seas and lakes.
The Biosphere in Balance
As the micro-organisms died, the cells piled up forming sedimentary rocks called stromatolites.
Some stromatolites show bands of iron oxides formed when iron ions combine with dissolved oxygen in the ocean.  Stromatolites with these bands are estimated to be 2.5 billion years old or more.
The Biosphere in Balance
This suggests that at this time, the level oxygen had started to increase.
Stromatolites that are less than 1.8 billion years old do not have black bands of iron oxides.

Scientists speculate that by this time most of the iron ions in the oceans were already bound as iron oxides.  With the ocean’s iron stores used up, the oxygen produced by photosynthesis was allowed to build up and escape into the atmosphere.
The Biosphere in Balance
Scientists think that the sudden increase in oxygen 2.5 billion years ago was mostly due to the activity of photosynthetic cyanobacteria.
The Biosphere in Balance
Over time species that were well adapted to life in the oxygen-rich biosphere evolved.
